name: Flu (influenza)
tagline: When to rest. When to call your doctor.

what_is_it.heading: Flu in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Influenza is a viral infection of the nose, throat, and lungs. It is far more aggressive than a common cold — fever, body aches, and exhaustion come on within hours.
paragraphs: Most healthy people recover within a week to ten days. The danger lies in complications — pneumonia, worsening of asthma or heart disease, dehydration in the elderly and young children. Roughly 11,000 South Africans die from flu-related complications every year.
Flu is not just a bad cold. Colds come on slowly. Flu hits within hours — high fever, dry cough, muscle aches, headaches, and the kind of exhaustion that puts you in bed.

items.headline: Seasonal
items.body: South African flu season runs roughly May to September. Get vaccinated in March or April.

items.headline: Still kills
items.body: Around 11,000 SA deaths a year — mostly from complications like pneumonia, mostly in the elderly and chronically ill.

items.headline: Free vaccine
items.body: High-risk groups get free flu vaccines at clinics — over 65, pregnant women, chronic illness, healthcare workers.

items.headline: Rest, not antibiotics
items.body: Healthy adults usually need rest, fluids, and time — not antibiotics. Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

pull_quote.text: The flu vaccine cannot give you flu — that is one of the most persistent and harmful myths. The vaccine contains no live virus.

signs.heading: Flu versus cold — how to tell
signs.lede: Flu and colds are different illnesses. Knowing which you have changes what you do next.

items.title: Flu hits fast and hard
items.description: High fever (over 38°C) coming on within hours, severe body aches, dry cough, exhaustion. You feel knocked over.

items.title: Cold builds slowly
items.description: Runny nose, sore throat, mild fatigue. You feel rough but functional. No high fever, no body aches.

items.title: Warning signs
items.description: Difficulty breathing, chest pain, blue lips, severe vomiting, confusion, symptoms that improve then suddenly get worse — see a clinic.

spreads.heading: How flu spreads
yes: Coughs and sneezes from infected people — droplets travel about a metre
Touching surfaces an infected person has coughed on, then touching your face
Close contact in poorly ventilated spaces — classrooms, taxis, offices
From an infected person starting a day before they feel sick
no: Getting cold or wet — the cold does not cause flu, the virus does
The flu vaccine — it contains no live virus

prevention.heading: How to protect yourself and your family
prevention.lede: The annual flu vaccine is the single most effective thing. Even if you still get flu after vaccination, it is usually much milder.

items.title: Annual flu vaccine
items.description: Get vaccinated every year before flu season. Free at clinics for high-risk groups, around R100 at most pharmacies for everyone else.

items.title: Wash hands often
items.description: Soap and water for 20 seconds, or alcohol sanitiser. Especially after public transport, shopping, or school pickup.

items.title: Ventilation
items.description: Open windows in homes, classrooms, and offices. Flu spreads far less in well-ventilated spaces.

items.title: Stay home if sick
items.description: If you have flu, stay home for 24 hours after your fever breaks. You are most infectious in the first 3–4 days.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.myth: The flu vaccine can give you flu.
items.fact: The flu vaccine contains no live virus. Some people feel tired or have a mild fever after the shot — that's the immune system responding, not flu.

items.myth: If I'm healthy, I don't need a flu vaccine.
items.fact: Healthy people usually survive flu — but spread it to more vulnerable people. Vaccination protects you and your children, parents, and colleagues.

items.myth: Antibiotics will clear my flu quickly.
items.fact: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. Flu is a virus. Taking antibiotics unnecessarily breeds resistant bacteria for later.

items.myth: Once I have symptoms, it's too late for the vaccine.
items.fact: If you already have flu, the vaccine won't cure that episode — but it's never too late for the season as a whole. There are often more exposures later.

items.title: Rest, fluids, paracetamol
items.description: Sleep as much as you can. Drink water, juice, soup. Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and aches.

items.title: Do not ask for antibiotics
items.description: Flu is viral. Antibiotics do nothing for viruses. They only help if a bacterial complication like pneumonia develops.

items.title: If high-risk — see a clinic early
items.description: Pregnant, over 65, chronic illness (asthma, heart disease, diabetes, HIV)? See a clinic within 48 hours — antivirals work best early.

items.title: Watch for warning signs
items.description: Difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, severe vomiting, sudden worsening — get medical attention.

items.title: Protect others
items.description: Stay home until fever-free for 24 hours. Cover coughs with your elbow. Do not visit elderly relatives while sick.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Most flu can be managed at home. Clinics and pharmacies help with severe symptoms and high-risk groups.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Every government clinic offers free flu vaccines for high-risk groups
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required
